title: Making karah prashad
hookLine: equal parts flour, sugar and butter, cooked while reciting

cards: Flour, sugar, butter. Three ingredients on a counter, and nothing about them looks holy. Then the flour goes into a heavy pan with the melted butter, and someone starts to stir.
It darkens slowly, pale to gold to the color of an old coin, and the kitchen fills with a warm, toasted smell. Sugar dissolved in water goes in with a hiss.
And all the while, the cook is saying something under their breath. Not a shopping list. Words of the Guru.
At the end of a gurdwara service, this is what lands in people's hands.

teach.h: KARAH PRASHAD: GRACE FROM THE PAN.
teach.b: Karah is the deep iron pan, and prashad is a gift given by grace: grace from the pan.

The Sikh Rehat Maryada gives the recipe, in paraphrase: equal parts wheat flour, sugar and clarified butter, prepared in a clean vessel by someone who has bathed, reciting Gurbani while it cooks. Start with the measure.
Equal parts: no ingredient is the star, and nothing a plain kitchen doesn't already have. Next, the cook. The code doesn't ask for a priest.
It asks for clean hands, a clean pot and a mind on the Guru's words. The prayer isn't added at the end like a garnish; it's stirred in the whole time. Then the bowl comes into the congregation.
The code describes stanzas of the Anand being recited and Ardas offered, and the prashad touched with a kirpan before it's shared. Last, the sharing.
The code says it's given to everyone in the sangat alike, without asking about caste.
Whoever you are, you hold out your hands, and the same sweet, warm handful lands in yours as in everyone else's. Some families make it at home too, with the same recipe and the same rule.
A kitchen becomes a place of remembrance, and an ordinary chore holds the Guru's words for as long as the pan is on the fire.

how: In gurdwaras, karah prashad is prepared from equal parts flour, sugar and ghee while Gurbani is recited, presented with Ardas, and handed to everyone in the congregation in cupped hands.

o: making the sweet offering while reciting Gurbani
frying sweets for a family wedding feast
boiling rice and lentils for the free kitchen

games.q: inside karah prashad: tap the pairs.

s: only a priest may make karah prashad
the code asks for clean hands, a clean vessel and Gurbani recited while cooking, not a priest.
the three ingredients go in equal parts
flour, sugar and clarified butter, in equal measure.
prashad is shared out by caste
the code says it is given to everyone in the sangat alike, without asking about caste.

games.q: you're making karah prashad for the sangat. when do the Guru's words come in?
o: they don't; it's just a recipe.
games.why: the code asks for Gurbani to be recited while it is prepared. the prayer is stirred in, not added at the end.

practice: Picture a small thing you'll cook soon, a pot of rice or a cup of tea, and choose the words you'd keep under your breath while you make it: a line of Gurbani, or simply Waheguru, if you pray; the names of the people who'll eat it, if not.
Then sit with your hands open in your lap, the way people hold them out for prashad, and walk through it once in your mind: the pan, the stirring, the words.

wordCard.voice: Making karah prashad. Equal parts flour, sugar and clarified butter, made with clean hands while reciting Gurbani, then shared with everyone alike. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: the sweet offering made in the karah, the iron pan, and given as grace.

carryVoice: Your line: pray while cooking. The prayer goes in with the flour, not after it. See you tomorrow.
